decisions.d1: Run a 3-week pilot with 12 technicians at the Newark warehouse.

a1.text: Send the proposal and pilot plan to Rachel

a3.text: Schedule a demo of offline mode for Harbor technicians

lines.speaker: Sofia Alvarez
lines.text: All right, I think we are all here. Rachel, James, it is so great to finally connect with you both. I know we've exchanged a few emails over the last couple of weeks, but it's great to do this face-to-face, or at least screen-to-screen. I've got Marcus Reid here with me from our Customer Success team. Marcus works super closely with our HVAC and mechanical clients, so I wanted him on the line to make sure we can speak to how our current customers are actually using the platform day-to-day.

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: Thanks, Sofia. Yeah, we've been looking forward to this. James and I actually just came from a scheduling meeting where we were dealing with the exact pain points we're hoping to talk about today. So the timing is pretty perfect.

lines.speaker: James Porter
lines.text: Absolutely. Thanks for having us. I'm hoping to get a good look at the technical architecture today if we have time, specifically around how you handle mobile device management and user provisioning, but I'll let Rachel kick off with the operational side first.

lines.speaker: Sofia Alvarez
lines.text: We will absolutely cover all of that, James. Marcus is a wizard with our MDM setups, and we can walk through exactly how we integrate with your stack. But to set the stage, I know from our brief email exchange that Harbor Logistics has about a hundred and forty field technicians doing commercial HVAC and industrial refrigeration maintenance. Rachel, maybe you can walk us through what a typical day looks like for your technicians right now, and where you're feeling the most friction?

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: Oh, where to begin. Honestly, Sofia, our biggest headache right now is paper. We are still, believe it or not, largely a paper-based operation when it comes to actual work orders in the field. Our dispatchers in the central office use a legacy scheduling software—it's this clunky desktop system we've had for ten years—and they print out physical work orders every morning. The technicians have to literally drive in, pick up their clipboards, go out to their sites, and then write everything down by hand.

lines.speaker: Marcus Reid
lines.text: That is incredibly common, Rachel. You'd be surprised how many of our forty-six current customers started in that exact same boat, with physical clipboards and morning drives just to get paper.

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: It is just killing our efficiency, Marcus. The technicians hate it because they're spenders, not writers. They want to turn wrenches, not fill out forms. So what happens is they scribble down the bare minimum. They might write 'replaced valve' but they won't write down the part number, or they'll forget to note how many hours they actually spent on site. Then, at the end of the week, they drop off this stack of crumpled, grease-stained papers on the dispatch desk.

lines.speaker: Sofia Alvarez
lines.text: And then I assume someone has to manually re-key all of that information into your billing system?

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: Exactly. We have two full-time administrative coordinators whose entire job is basically translating technician handwriting and manual data entry. It's incredibly slow. Sometimes a work order doesn't get billed until three weeks after the job is actually completed because we're waiting to clarify what a technician wrote. And if a technician wrote down the wrong part number, we have to call them, they don't remember, and it's just this massive game of telephone.

lines.speaker: Marcus Reid
lines.text: Right, and during those three weeks, you have zero visibility into what work was actually completed or what parts are sitting in your inventory, which must make stock tracking a nightmare.

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: It's a total black box, Marcus. We have no idea what inventory is actually on the trucks versus what's still in our main warehouse. But the absolute worst part of this paper system is what we call the 'second visit rate.' Right now, about fifteen percent of our jobs require a second visit because the technician didn't have the right historical data on the customer's system when they arrived, or they didn't know which specific refrigerant model was installed on that specific warehouse roof. So they show up, realize they don't have the right tools or information, and have to schedule a follow-up.

lines.speaker: Sofia Alvarez
lines.text: Fifteen percent is a huge number when you have one hundred and forty technicians out in the field. That is a massive amount of lost revenue and wasted windshield time. If we could get that fifteen percent down to, say, three or four percent, what would that mean for your bottom line?

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: Oh, it would be massive. I mean, just in terms of fuel costs and technician hours, we're talking hundreds of thousands of dollars a year. Not to mention customer satisfaction. Our clients are large-scale logistics and cold-storage warehouses. If their industrial refrigeration goes down, they are losing thousands of dollars of perishable inventory every single hour. They don't have time for us to make two visits because our tech didn't know what compressor model was installed.

lines.speaker: James Porter
lines.text: And if I can jump in here, from an IT perspective, the current process is also a security nightmare. Technicians are writing down customer gate codes, security PINs, and facility contacts on these paper work orders. If a tech loses a clipboard at a coffee shop, that is a direct physical security breach for our clients. We have no way to wipe that data or secure it. That's one of the big reasons I'm pushing for a secure mobile solution.

lines.speaker: Sofia Alvarez
lines.text: That makes total sense, James. Security is at the core of how we built Tidewater. Every single piece of data stored on our mobile app is encrypted at rest, and we support full remote data wiping if a device is lost or stolen. We can get into those specific protocols in a minute, but I want to make sure I understand the environment your techs are working in. Rachel, you mentioned cold-storage warehouses. I imagine those facilities have some pretty tough cellular coverage?

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: Absolutely. It is a complete dead zone. These warehouses are basically giant insulated metal boxes. Once our technicians step inside, or go down into the basement mechanical rooms, they have absolutely zero cellular signal. No 5G, no Wi-Fi, nothing. And this is where previous software trials have completely fallen on their face for us. We tried a pilot with another mobile tool last year, and the moment the tech lost signal, the app would freeze, they couldn't access the work order details, and they couldn't save their progress. It was a disaster. The techs literally refused to use it.

lines.speaker: James Porter
lines.text: Yeah, that pilot was a mess. The app kept trying to ping the cloud server for every single button press. When it couldn't establish a handshake, it would just throw timeout errors and discard the locally cached data. We ended up having to manually clean up database conflicts for a month after we pulled the plug on that pilot. So, James here is extremely skeptical of any vendor who claims they have an 'offline mode' until we see exactly how it works under the hood.

lines.speaker: Sofia Alvarez
lines.text: I completely understand that skepticism, James, and honestly, you have every right to be skeptical. A lot of field service apps were built for suburban residential plumbing where you almost always have some signal, and then they tried to patch on an offline mode later as an afterthought. Tidewater was designed from day one with a local-first architecture. This means our mobile app functions entirely independently of an active internet connection.

lines.speaker: Marcus Reid
lines.text: To give you a practical example of how this works, James, our app maintains a fully functional local SQLite database on the technician's device. When a technician downloads their schedule for the day in the morning while they have Wi-Fi at home or at the office, the app pulls down all the historical work orders, equipment specs, and customer history for those specific sites. Once they are inside that cold-storage facility with zero signal, the app doesn't need to talk to the server at all.

lines.speaker: James Porter
lines.text: Okay, but what happens when they make changes offline? If they update a work order, log parts used, or take photos of a damaged compressor coil, where does that data go, and how do you handle conflict resolution when they eventually regain a connection?

lines.speaker: Marcus Reid
lines.text: Great question. All of those updates, photos, and time logs are written immediately to that local SQLite database on the device. The app tracks every change in a local transaction queue. When the technician walks out of the warehouse and their phone picks up a cellular signal—even just a weak 3G connection—the app automatically begins background synchronization. It pushes those queued transactions up to our cloud servers in small, compressed packets so it doesn't hog bandwidth.

lines.speaker: James Porter
lines.text: And if two technicians are working on the same site and both make offline changes to the same asset, how do you resolve those overlapping writes without corrupting the database?

lines.speaker: Marcus Reid
lines.text: We use a last-write-wins resolution strategy by default, timestamped at the device level, but we also flag any concurrent updates in the dispatcher portal. So if there is a conflict, the dispatch team gets a clear notification to review and confirm the change. In reality, because technicians are assigned to specific work orders individually, true write conflicts are actually quite rare, representing less than zero point five percent of all sync transactions across our entire customer base. But we have the safety nets in place to handle them gracefully.

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: That is a huge relief to hear, Marcus. Our technicians cannot be expected to manage sync errors. If they see a red error screen, they will just put the phone in their pocket and go back to writing things on their hands or on scraps of cardboard. It has to be completely seamless for them.

lines.speaker: Sofia Alvarez
lines.text: And that is exactly our philosophy, Rachel. The technician experience has to be friction-free. If the app isn't easier than paper, they won't use it, and then the whole system falls apart. That's why we designed our interface with giant buttons that can be tapped even if a technician is wearing work gloves, and we support speech-to-text so they can dictate their service notes rather than typing them out on a tiny virtual keyboard.

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: Speech-to-text would be amazing. Some of our older technicians struggle with smartphone screens, so being able to just talk to the app and say 'replaced the compressor fan belt' would save them so much frustration. What about photos? Can they attach photos directly to the work order while offline?

lines.speaker: Marcus Reid
lines.text: Yes, absolutely. They can snap photos directly within the Tidewater app. The app automatically compresses the images locally so they don't eat up the device's storage or take forever to upload once they regain connection. Those photos are pinned directly to the specific asset record and the work order, so when Rachel's team in the back office reviews the job, they can see the exact before-and-after photos of the equipment. It makes customer billing disputes practically disappear because you have photographic proof of the work done.

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: Oh, we get those disputes all the time. A customer will claim we didn't actually replace a filter, and we have no way to prove we did without sending someone back out or digging through old physical parts. Having a timestamped, geotagged photo attached to the digital invoice would save us so many awkward phone calls.

lines.speaker: Sofia Alvarez
lines.text: Exactly. It completely changes the relationship with your customers. You go from 'trust us, we did the work' to 'here is the exact digital record, the technician's notes, the exact timestamps, and the photos of the completed job.' It builds a massive amount of trust.

lines.speaker: James Porter
lines.text: Let's talk about the devices themselves. Our technicians are currently split. About sixty percent of them have company-issued iPhones, and the other forty percent are using their personal Android devices under our Bring Your Own Device policy. We manage all corporate-owned devices through Microsoft Intune. James, how does Tidewater handle MDM deployment, and do you support containerization for BYOD users?

lines.speaker: Marcus Reid
lines.text: We are fully compatible with Microsoft Intune, James. We can deliver our app as a wrapped package that you can deploy directly through your Intune App SDK. This allows you to enforce your standard security policies, like preventing copy-paste of customer data outside of the managed container, requiring a separate PIN to open the app, and forcing data encryption at rest on those personal Android devices.

lines.speaker: James Porter
lines.text: That's excellent. What about user provisioning and single sign-on? We use Azure Active Directory, now Microsoft Entra ID, for all of our corporate identity management. I do not want to manage another set of credentials for one hundred and forty field users. If a technician leaves the company, I need to be able to revoke their access instantly from my centralized Entra console.

lines.speaker: Sofia Alvarez
lines.text: We hear you loud and clear on that, James. We support SAML 2.0 and OIDC integrations out of the box for Single Sign-On. You can connect your Entra ID directly to Tidewater. This means your technicians use their existing corporate credentials to log in, and the moment you deactivate a user in Entra, their access to Tidewater is instantly revoked on all devices, and any cached data on their personal phone is automatically wiped during the next handshake attempt.

lines.speaker: James Porter
lines.text: Okay, that's exactly what I needed to hear on the identity side. What about system updates? Because our techs are out in the field all day, we can't have the app forcing a major update in the middle of a shift that blocks them from seeing their schedules. How do you handle app store updates and backward compatibility with your backend APIs?

lines.speaker: Marcus Reid
lines.text: We maintain strict API backward compatibility for at least three major versions, James. This means if a technician has auto-updates turned off on their personal phone and is running an app version that is six months old, it will still communicate perfectly with our cloud servers without any data loss. When we do release critical security patches, we have a feature in our admin console that allows you to set a 'minimum required version' which will gently prompt the user to update at the end of their shift, rather than locking them out when they are standing on a roof in the middle of a service call.

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: That is really smart, Marcus. Our guys would lose their minds if they got locked out of their schedule at eight in the morning because of an automatic update. I want to make sure we talk about the dispatch side of things too. Right now, our dispatchers are using a legacy system that is very manual. How does Tidewater handle the actual scheduling and assignment of jobs?

lines.speaker: Sofia Alvarez
lines.text: Our dispatcher console is completely web-based, Rachel. It gives your coordinators a real-time map view of where all one hundred and forty technicians are located, based on their last synced GPS coordinates. When a new emergency service call comes in, the dispatcher can instantly see who is closest, who has the right certifications for that specific refrigeration system, and who has free space on their schedule. They can drag and drop the job directly onto the technician's calendar, and the technician gets an instant push notification on their phone.

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: And does that sync with their mobile calendar, or do they have to stay inside your app to see their schedule?

lines.speaker: Marcus Reid
lines.text: They can view it entirely inside the Tidewater app, which we highly recommend because it links directly to the turn-by-turn navigation, the customer's equipment history, and the digital safety checklists they have to complete before they start the job. But we can also export a read-only sync feed to Apple Calendar or Google Calendar if they want to see their work schedule alongside their personal commitments.

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: Those digital safety checklists are actually something our compliance team has been asking for, Marcus. Right now, we have these safety forms that the techs are supposed to sign before they touch any high-voltage electrical panels or heavy refrigeration equipment. But again, with paper, they just check all the boxes at the end of the week without actually doing the checks. Can we enforce those safety steps in the app?

lines.speaker: Sofia Alvarez
lines.text: Yes, absolutely. We call those 'conditional workflows.' You can configure the app so that a technician cannot physically open the work order or start logging their time until they have completed the safety checklist. You can even require them to upload a photo of their lock-out, tag-out safety lock on the electrical breaker before the app unlocks the next step of the service call. It is a fantastic way to ensure 100% compliance with OSHA and your internal safety protocols.

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: That is incredible. That would make our safety officer incredibly happy. He's been terrified of the liability of our current 'pencil-whipping' culture when it comes to those paper safety forms.

lines.speaker: James Porter
lines.text: I like the sound of that too. Sofia, how does your system handle data extraction if we need to run custom analytics? We use Power BI for our corporate reporting. We track metrics like first-time fix rate, average resolution time, and technician utilization. Can we query your database directly, or do you have a robust API we can tap into?

lines.speaker: Sofia Alvarez
lines.text: We have a fully documented REST API that gives you access to every single data point in Tidewater, James. You can pull work order statuses, technician hours, parts utilized, and customer feedback directly into your Power BI warehouse. We also support webhook notifications, so you can set up real-time triggers. For example, the moment a technician marks a job as 'completed' in the field, our system can send a webhook to your billing software to automatically generate the invoice, without waiting for any manual intervention.

lines.speaker: James Porter
lines.text: That webhook capability would save my development team a ton of time. We've had to write custom polling scripts for our other legacy systems, and they are incredibly fragile. Webhooks are a much cleaner way to handle real-time integration.

lines.speaker: Marcus Reid
lines.text: Absolutely, James. And since we have forty-six customers running this exact system, we've already built out standard integration templates for most of the major ERP and accounting platforms. Depending on what you are using for your backend billing, we might have an out-of-the-box connector ready to go, which would save your team from having to write any custom integration code at all.

lines.speaker: James Porter
lines.text: We are currently on Microsoft Dynamics 365 for our financial back office. Do you have a connector for Dynamics?

lines.speaker: Sofia Alvarez
lines.text: We do! We have a pre-built integration framework for Dynamics 365 that handles account synchronization, inventory levels, and invoice generation. We can walk through that in detail during our next technical session, but it essentially allows you to keep Dynamics as your single source of truth for financial data, while Tidewater serves as the high-speed engine for your field operations.

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: This all sounds amazing, Sofia, but I have to ask about the onboarding process. Our technicians are not software engineers. Some of them have been with us for twenty-five years and are incredibly set in their ways. If this rollout is painful, or if they feel like we are micromanaging them with GPS tracking, we're going to face a lot of pushback. How do you help companies transition from paper to digital without losing half their staff in the process?

lines.speaker: Marcus Reid
lines.text: Rachel, that is probably the most important question you could ask. Software is only as good as its adoption rate. If your technicians reject it, the project is a failure, no matter how good our APIs are. That's why my team doesn't just hand you a login and wish you luck. We partner with you to design a phased rollout plan.

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: What does a phased rollout look like in practice?

lines.speaker: Marcus Reid
lines.text: We typically start with what we call a 'champion pilot.' We identify five or six of your most respected, influential technicians—often the ones who are natural leaders on the team, regardless of their tech-savviness. We get them on the app first, we sit with them, and we make sure they feel completely comfortable. Once they see how much faster they can complete their paperwork, they start telling the other guys in the breakroom, 'Hey, this app actually saves me an hour of admin time every day.' That peer-to-peer recommendation is worth a thousand training manuals.

lines.speaker: Sofia Alvarez
lines.text: And to add to that, Rachel, we also run virtual training clinics specifically tailored for field staff. We don't do boring PowerPoint presentations. We do live, interactive sessions where they have the app on their own phones, and we walk them through completing a dummy work order, taking a photo, and logging their time. We make it fun, we keep it simple, and we show them exactly what is in it for them—which is less paperwork, fewer phone calls from angry dispatchers, and getting to go home on time at the end of the day.

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: That sounds like a really thoughtful approach. I like the idea of starting with a pilot team. It would give us a chance to iron out any operational wrinkles before we try to train all one hundred and forty techs at once.

lines.speaker: James Porter
lines.text: And from my side, it lets me test the security policies and the Intune containerization on a small group of users before we push it out to the entire fleet. It's much easier to debug MDM profile issues on five devices than on a hundred and forty.

lines.speaker: Sofia Alvarez
lines.text: Absolutely, James. We can set up a dedicated staging environment for your IT team during the pilot, so you can test all the provisioning, SSO handshakes, and Intune security wrappers without affecting any live production data. We want to make sure you are 100% confident in the security architecture before a single real customer work order is processed.

lines.speaker: James Porter
lines.text: That's exactly what I wanted to hear. If we can lock down the staging environment and run a clean pilot, my team will be fully on board.

lines.speaker: Sofia Alvarez
lines.text: Fantastic. Well, we've covered a lot of ground today on the operational challenges with your paper system, the fifteen percent second-visit rate, the critical need for a robust offline database in those metal cold-storage facilities, and the security requirements around Microsoft Intune and Entra ID. This has been incredibly helpful for us to understand your environment.

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: It's been really helpful for us too, Sofia. It feels like you guys actually understand the reality of field service work, rather than just trying to sell us a generic CRM tool that doesn't work in a basement.

lines.speaker: Sofia Alvarez
lines.text: We live and breathe field service, Rachel. It's all we do. I want to respect everyone's time, so I think we should transition to showing you a live demo of the actual mobile interface and the dispatcher dashboard, so you can see exactly what we've been talking about in action. Marcus has a demo environment set up, so we can walk through a simulated HVAC service call from start to finish, including simulating a total loss of cellular signal. How does that sound?

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: That sounds perfect. Let's see the actual app.

lines.speaker: Sofia Alvarez
lines.text: Awesome, Marcus, do you want to share your screen and jump right into the dispatcher console first? We can show Rachel and James how the back-office dispatch team coordinates with the field technicians in real time, especially when job changes happen on the fly.

lines.speaker: Marcus Reid
lines.text: You bet. Let me share my screen here. Let me know when you can see the clean grid layout of the dispatcher dashboard.

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: Yes, we can see it. It looks much cleaner than our current whiteboard system, that's for sure.

lines.speaker: Marcus Reid
lines.text: Thanks, Rachel. That whiteboard pain is exactly what we aim to eliminate. On the left here, you see your incoming work orders, which can be ingested directly from Dynamics 365 or created manually by your dispatch team. On the right, you see your technicians mapped in real time based on their active status.

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: Look at those map pins. Are those real-time GPS locations of the technicians, or just where their last job was?

lines.speaker: Marcus Reid
lines.text: They are active GPS locations, but they only poll when a technician is actively clocked into a shift on the mobile app. We respect their privacy, so once they clock out at the end of the day, the location tracking stops completely. Our unionized clients really appreciate that boundary.

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: That's perfect. Our union representatives will definitely ask about that, so having a hard stop on tracking at clock-out is a major selling point.

lines.speaker: James Porter
lines.text: How often does the GPS ping the server, Marcus? And what is the average data payload size for those pings? We need to keep cellular data usage in mind for our mobile plans.

lines.speaker: Marcus Reid
lines.text: It pings every five minutes by default, James, but that is fully configurable in your admin settings. The data payload is incredibly lightweight—under two kilobytes per ping—so even over a full month of active shifts, it uses less than a couple of megabytes of cellular data per device.

lines.speaker: James Porter
lines.text: Okay, that is negligible. That's great to hear.

lines.speaker: Marcus Reid
lines.text: Now, let's look at the mobile app side. I'm going to pull up my simulated iPhone screen here. This is exactly what the technician sees when they log in. They get their daily schedule, a list of parts required for their assigned jobs, and customer contact information.

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: And how do they log parts used on-site? Right now, they write parts on a paper slip, and half the time, the handwriting is so bad we can't read the serial numbers, which means we miss out on billing the customer for those parts.

lines.speaker: Marcus Reid
lines.text: I hear that story almost every week, Rachel. In Tidewater, the technician simply taps 'Add Parts' on the work order, and they can search your live inventory catalog. They can also use their phone's camera to scan the barcode or QR code on the refrigeration unit or part box, and the system automatically matches the exact serial number and adds it to the digital invoice.

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: Wow, barcode scanning directly from the phone camera? That alone could save us thousands in unbilled inventory every month.

lines.speaker: Sofia Alvarez
lines.text: It really does, Rachel! We have one customer in Ohio who saw a twenty-two percent increase in billed inventory within the first sixty days of launching Tidewater, just because the techs didn't have to write down serial numbers manually anymore.

lines.speaker: James Porter
lines.text: Let's talk about offline functionality. You mentioned earlier that the app works in basements and deep freeze warehouses. What happens when there is absolutely no cell signal? Does the technician lose access to the parts database?

lines.speaker: Marcus Reid
lines.text: Not at all, James. This is where our unique local SQLite architecture shines. I'll simulate a total loss of cellular signal right now by toggling airplane mode on this device. You'll see the status bar at the top turn amber, indicating the app is in offline mode.

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: And the app doesn't freeze or crash?

lines.speaker: Marcus Reid
lines.text: Nope, it's completely seamless. The technician can still view all their job details, update the work order status, add parts, type up their service notes, and even capture the customer's signature. Everything is saved locally to their device's encrypted storage.

lines.speaker: James Porter
lines.text: Wait, how secure is that local storage? If a technician loses their phone at a diner, is that cached database encrypted on the physical device?

lines.speaker: Marcus Reid
lines.text: Yes, James, absolutely. We use SQLCipher to encrypt the local SQLite database using AES 256-bit encryption. The encryption key is generated dynamically based on the user's authenticated session, so if they lose the device and the session expires, the database is completely unreadable, even if someone attempts to extract the storage chip.

lines.speaker: James Porter
lines.text: Okay, that's a solid answer. We use Microsoft Intune for our MDM. Can we enforce app-level PINs and containerization on the Tidewater app?

lines.speaker: Marcus Reid
lines.text: Yes, we are fully compatible with Microsoft Intune app protection policies. You can prevent data copy-paste between Tidewater and personal apps, enforce biometrics or PIN to open the app, and remotely wipe the local data if a device is reported lost.

lines.speaker: James Porter
lines.text: That's exactly what I needed to hear. That takes care of our mobile device security concerns.

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: And what happens to the data once the technician gets back into cell range? Does it sync automatically, or do they have to press a button?

lines.speaker: Marcus Reid
lines.text: It syncs completely automatically in the background, Rachel. The moment the app detects a stable cellular or Wi-Fi connection, it securely pushes the queued updates back to the Tidewater cloud, which then updates the dispatcher console and syncs the completed work order back to Dynamics 365.

lines.speaker: James Porter
lines.text: What about synchronization conflicts? For example, if a tech is working offline in a basement for three hours, and during that time, a dispatcher edits the same work order back in the office, how does Tidewater handle that conflict when the tech comes back online?

lines.speaker: Marcus Reid
lines.text: That's a classic synchronization challenge. We handle it through a deterministic conflict resolution engine. By default, we use a last-write-wins model based on the exact timestamp of the action, but if there is a direct conflict—say, the dispatcher changed the assigned asset while the tech was servicing it—the system marks the work order for administrative review. The dispatcher sees a notification flag, and they can manually verify and approve which changes to keep.

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: That makes sense. We can't have our dispatchers blindly overwriting the actual field data, so having a manual review flag is really smart.

lines.speaker: James Porter
lines.text: Let's move to identity management. SSO with Azure AD is a hard requirement before rollout for us. We do not support managing standalone passwords for our technicians. Is that supported out of the box?

lines.speaker: Sofia Alvarez
lines.text: Yes, James, SSO with Azure AD is fully supported. We integrate directly with Microsoft Entra ID using SAML 2.0 or OpenID Connect. We can set up the configuration within your tenant in about thirty minutes, and it supports multi-factor authentication seamlessly through whatever policies you already have active in your Azure tenant.

lines.speaker: James Porter
lines.text: And does it support automatic user provisioning? If we add a technician to our Azure AD group, does that auto-create their account in Tidewater, or do we have to manually create them?

lines.speaker: Marcus Reid
lines.text: Yes, we support SCIM provisioning, James. So when you assign a user to the Tidewater group in Azure AD, their profile is automatically created in Tidewater. When they leave the company or change roles, disabling them in Azure AD instantly revokes their access to Tidewater and wipes their local database on the next app launch.

lines.speaker: James Porter
lines.text: Excellent. That saves my team from dealing with manual onboarding tickets for new hires.

lines.speaker: Sofia Alvarez
lines.text: Exactly, James. We want to make IT administration as hands-off as possible. Now, Rachel, I know we've talked a lot about the technology, but I want to make sure we are aligned on the commercial side. You mentioned that you have budget approval for Q1. Can you share what your target budget looks like for this transition?

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: Yes, absolutely. Our budget is approved for Q1, around ninety thousand dollars per year. That needs to cover the annual software subscription, our integration maintenance, and any initial deployment fees. Is that a realistic budget for a fleet of one hundred and forty technicians on Tidewater?

lines.speaker: Sofia Alvarez
lines.text: That is absolutely realistic, Rachel. In fact, we can structure our enterprise licensing to fit beautifully right into that ninety thousand dollar annual target. Our standard pricing for one hundred and forty technicians, including full access to our offline-first mobile app, the dispatcher dashboard, and our Microsoft Dynamics integration framework, will easily align with your parameters.

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: That's a huge relief, Sofia. We really don't have the flexibility to go over that ninety thousand limit, and going back to the board to ask for more money would delay this whole project by six months.

lines.speaker: Sofia Alvarez
lines.text: We completely understand. We will make sure our final proposal is fully optimized to fit within your budget constraints, with no hidden surprises or overage fees.

lines.speaker: James Porter
lines.text: Before we go any further, what does the official decision process look like on your side? Who else do we need to bring into this conversation?

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: Well, as Director of Operations, I am the economic buyer and the ultimate operational decision-maker for this project. If I say we go with Tidewater, that's our operational choice. However, James has veto power on the technology side. James must pass the security review and confirm that the integration architecture is safe and compliant before we can move to a contract.

lines.speaker: James Porter
lines.text: Right. If Tidewater fails our security review, or if the SSO integration isn't stable, we can't move forward. But based on what you've shown me so far, I'm confident we can clear those hurdles.

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: And once James signs off on security and I approve the product fit, it goes to our CFO, Robert, who signs the actual contract. Robert is extremely thorough, so he will want to see clear evidence of a successful pilot and a defined ROI before he signs on the dotted line.

lines.speaker: Sofia Alvarez
lines.text: That's a very standard process, Rachel. We love working with CFOs like Robert because the return on investment with Tidewater is so clear. Between eliminating lost parts billing and saving an hour of admin time per technician every day, the app practically pays for itself in the first quarter.

lines.speaker: Marcus Reid
lines.text: And to help you build that business case for Robert, we recommend a very structured onboarding process. We use a proven thirty-day rollout plan that minimizes operational risk and ensures high user adoption from day one.

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: Thirty days? That sounds incredibly fast for a team of one hundred and forty technicians who are mostly used to paper. How does that actually work without causing chaos in our operations?

lines.speaker: Marcus Reid
lines.text: It works because we don't try to train and transition all one hundred and forty technicians on day one. Our thirty-day rollout plan is divided into four distinct weekly phases. Phase one is the technical setup and Dynamics database mapping, which we do with James. Phase two is our 'champion pilot' where we train a small, select group of your top technicians.

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: And what happens in week three?

lines.speaker: Marcus Reid
lines.text: Phase three is feedback and configuration tuning. We gather real-world input from the pilot team, adjust the interface layout based on their feedback, and prepare our final training materials. Then, phase four, week four, is the full fleet rollout and go-live, where we support your team with active live support channels.

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: I really like that phased approach, Marcus. It makes a lot of sense. If we are going to do this, we should start with a pilot team at our Newark warehouse.

lines.speaker: Sofia Alvarez
lines.text: Why Newark specifically, Rachel?

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: Newark is our largest and most challenging depot. We have twelve technicians there who handle our toughest industrial refrigeration accounts. They deal with concrete walls, deep-freeze environments, and very demanding customers. If Tidewater can handle the Newark workload and if those twelve technicians buy into it, the rest of the fleet will fall in line immediately.

lines.speaker: Marcus Reid
lines.text: That is an excellent strategy, Rachel. If you can prove success in your toughest facility, the rest of the rollout will be incredibly smooth. I highly recommend that.

lines.speaker: James Porter
lines.text: And from my side, the Newark group is perfect because they are already equipped with our corporate-managed iPhones. It gives me a clean, controlled group of users to test our Intune configuration and SSO policies in real-world conditions.

lines.speaker: Sofia Alvarez
lines.text: I completely agree. This is the perfect scope for a proof of concept. Let's make that our path forward.

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: Yes, let's make that official. We will run a three-week pilot with twelve technicians at the Newark warehouse.

lines.speaker: Marcus Reid
lines.text: I think that is the perfect decision. Run a three-week pilot with twelve technicians at the Newark warehouse. That gives us enough time to gather solid performance data, and it keeps the scope manageable for feedback loops.

lines.speaker: James Porter
lines.text: I agree. That's a solid plan that lets me test the security infrastructure without overwhelming our IT support desk.

lines.speaker: Sofia Alvarez
lines.text: Wonderful! We have a solid agreement here. Let's list out our next steps and assign some clear action items so we can maintain this great momentum.

lines.speaker: Sofia Alvarez
lines.text: I'll go first. Sofia Alvarez will send the proposal and pilot plan to Rachel by Friday. I'll make sure it clearly outlines the licensing fees, the Dynamics integration setup, and the specific timeline for the Newark pilot.

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: Excellent, Sofia. I will look out for that on Friday. If you can get it to me by then, I'll review it over the weekend so we can discuss it early next week.

lines.speaker: James Porter
lines.text: And on my end, I need to get our security compliance team involved. James Porter will send Tidewater the security questionnaire by Monday. Sofia, should I send that directly to you?

lines.speaker: Sofia Alvarez
lines.text: Yes, please send it straight to my email, James. Our security operations team will jump on it immediately, and we will get it returned to you within forty-eight hours.

lines.speaker: James Porter
lines.text: Perfect, I'll have that over to you on Monday morning.

lines.speaker: Marcus Reid
lines.text: And before we kick off the actual pilot with the team in Newark, I want to make sure the technicians themselves have a chance to see how the app works in real time, especially the offline database functionality. Marcus Reid will schedule a demo of offline mode for Harbor technicians by next week.

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: That's an excellent idea, Marcus. Getting our technicians comfortable with the offline mode early will prevent a lot of anxiety and build excitement before the launch. I'll coordinate with the Newark depot supervisor to find a thirty-minute window when the techs are in the office next week.

lines.speaker: Marcus Reid
lines.text: That sounds perfect, Rachel. I will send over a few calendar options so you can coordinate with the supervisor.

lines.speaker: Sofia Alvarez
lines.text: This has been an absolutely fantastic session today. I am so excited about this partnership, and I'm confident we are going to make a massive impact on your field operations.

lines.speaker: Rachel Kim
lines.text: Thank you, everyone. This was extremely helpful and productive.

lines.speaker: James Porter
lines.text: Yes, thank you all. I appreciate the thorough answers to my technical questions. Talk soon.

lines.speaker: Marcus Reid
lines.text: Thanks, everyone! Have a great afternoon.
